subject: Banking
title: High-Frequency Trading
description: A quick win: understand High-Frequency Trading.

hook.text: High-frequency traders execute thousands of trades per second using algorithms.

buildup.text: HFT firms spend millions on faster connections. A fiber optic cable from Chicago to New York shaved 3 milliseconds off.

discovery.text: HFT provides liquidity and tightens spreads. Average investors get slightly better prices because of algorithm.

twist.text: The 2010 Flash Crash saw the Dow drop 1,000 points in minutes.

climax.text: HFT makes markets faster and cheaper daily but dangerous in crisis. Speed helps in calm and hurts in panic.

punchline.text: Thousands of trades per second, pennies each. Speed is profit and peril.

quiz.question: What caused the 2010 Flash Crash?
options: HFT algorithms amplifying a sell-off faster than humans could intervene

details.summary: High-frequency trading uses powerful computers and algorithms to execute thousands of trades per second, exploiting tiny price differences across markets. HFT firms now account for roughly half of all US stock trading volume.
details.whyItMatters: HFT has fundamentally changed market structure, providing liquidity and tighter spreads while raising concerns about flash crashes, unfair speed advantages, and whether markets serve investors or algorithm operators.
takeaways: HFT firms execute trades in microseconds using co-located servers
They profit from tiny price differences across exchanges and instruments
The 2010 Flash Crash briefly wiped out nearly a trillion dollars in value

faq.question: Is high-frequency trading legal?
faq.answer: Yes, though heavily regulated. Certain practices like spoofing, where fake orders are placed to manipulate prices, are illegal. Legitimate HFT strategies that provide liquidity and improve price discovery are permitted.

faq.question: Does high-frequency trading hurt regular investors?
faq.answer: It depends on the strategy. Market-making HFT narrows bid-ask spreads, benefiting all investors. But predatory strategies that front-run orders exploit slower traders, effectively extracting value from institutional and retail investors.
